list.listitem: Nonsurgical therapy is effective in reducing periodontal disease. A
Failure to monitor patients’ periodontal disease may lead to uncontrolled disease and tooth loss. C
Older patients are insensitive to temperature changes and other symptoms of periodontal disease and need closer follow up. C
Gingivitis is a reversible condition. C
Decreasing consumption of foods with high sugar content can improve oral health. B

background.definition: Periodontal disease occurs when colonies of microorganisms (plaques) form on the teeth near the gingiva and between the gingiva and the root surface within the gingival sulcus. Gingivitis is an inflammation limited to the gingiva. It is the most common form of periodontal disease. A patient with gingivitis has no destruction of the periodontal fibers or bone that support the teeth.

list.listitem: Dentate adults: prevalence of active periodontitis is 20% to 49%.
Black and Hispanic Americans have a significantly higher prevalence of advanced periodontitis than do white Americans.

Prevalence of periodontitis in NHANES III was 11.4% for Blacks, followed by Mexican-Americans 6.9% and that of whites as 6.7%. In general, the blacks and Mexican-Americans were of lower education and lower income level, with higher incidence of diabetes and smoking than the whites.
Overall prevalence of periodontitis decreased between NHANES III and NHANES II 1999 to 2000.
Children: the prevalence of gingivitis in a national survey ranged from 40% to 60%.

Periodontal disease has been associated with preterm low-birth-weight infants, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes (although causality has not been established, and evidence does not support treatment to prevent preterm birth).
It tends to be more severe in patients with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus.
A Cochrane review determined that scaling and root planing (SRP) has a small effective on glycemic control (0.29%) in type II diabetics that lasts for approximately 4 months.
Epidemiological data correlates osteoporosis and tooth loss due to periodontitis.
Poor oral hygiene.
Dental plaque.

Dominant bacterial species associated with gingivitis are Gram-positive anaerobes, for example, Actinomyces viscosus and Peptostreptococcus micros and Gram-negative species (eg, Campylobacter gracilis, Fusobacterium nucleatum, Prevotella intermedia, and Veillonella).
It can also occur at puberty, during a menstrual cycle and pregnancy.
Gingivitis can also be an early sign of a systemic disorder like diabetes, AIDS, and vitamin deficiency. Severe deficiency of Vitamin C or niacin can cause gingivitis.
Some patients with Crohn’s disease may have inflammation during flare ups.
Exposure to heavy metals like lead and bismuth may cause gingivitis with a dark line at the margin.
In an analysis of 21 case-control studies, the odds ratio (OR) of detection of Ebsten-Barr virus DNA and the presence of periodontal disease was 6.2.

Gingivitis is caused by bacterial plaque that accumulates on the teeth. The same plaque hardens in 48 to 72 hours and forms calculus. The calculus becomes a nidus for plaque accumulation and the inflammation worsens.
Gingival overgrowth may be caused by inhibition of collagen phagocytosis by reduction of alpha2 integrin expression in gingival fibroblasts.
Local and systemic factors can modify the response of the periodontal tissues to plaque.
Antimicrobial mouth rinses and toothpaste reduce the bacterial count and inhibit bacterial activity in dental plaque, which causes gingivitis. C

Brush teeth twice a day with an ADA-accepted fluoride toothpaste. Replace tooth brush every 3 to 4 months or sooner if bristles are frayed. Powered rotation oscillation brushes may reduce gingivitis more effectively than manual tooth brushing or powered side-to-side brushes. Clean between teeth daily with floss or other inter dental aids. Eat a balanced diet and limit between-meal snacks.
C
Although scaling and polishing at regular intervals are routinely recommended, especially for patients at high risk for periodontal disease, there is no clear evidence to support its efficacy. B
Encourage smoking cessation to improve periodontal health and to reduce tooth loss in heavy smokers of cigarettes, cigars, and pipes with periodontal disease. C
Clinical parameter of bleeding on probing is a reliable tool for diagnosing gingival inflammation. C

Diagnosis is based on clinical traditional assessment including: (1) presence or absence of clinical signs of inflammation (eg, bleeding), (2) probing depths, (3) extent and pattern of loss of clinical attachment and bone, (4) patients’ medical and dental histories, and (5) presence of pain, ulceration, calculus, or plaque. C
Patients with gingivitis may present with complains of swollen and bleeding gums. They may also complain of bad breath. Many will remain asymptomatic.

Bleeding can occur spontaneously or while brushing and/or eating. Bleeding gums may be a complaint during puberty, pregnancy, or even be related to the menstrual cycle. If the complaint is related to these then the only measure that needs to be taken is an improvement of oral hygiene.
It is also necessary to know if this complaint is recurrent and what the patient has done for it in the past.
It is important to know how often the patient brushes his/her teeth, and what other oral hygiene aids he/she uses.
Take a history of smoking. Cigarette smoking compromises the periodontal health and may cause bleeding gums.
A detailed dental history should include the last time that the patient visited a dentist. This will also show his or her level of interest in improving his/her own oral hygiene.

After taking the above history, perform a detailed dental examination. If the patient wears dentures have them remove them. Inspect the oral cavity for general oral hygiene of the patient. Look for tooth decay or broken down teeth. Look for obvious plaque and tartar deposits. Look at the general condition of the gums. Is there inflammation and swelling of the gingiva? If present, is it generalized or localized. If localized, note down which teeth it is localized to. Juvenile periodontitis, which may initially present as red, swollen bleeding gums is a rapidly progressive disease limited to the incisors and molars. If there is suspicion of juvenile periodontitis, refer to a dentist immediately.

Palpate the gums, especially around the necks of the teeth. Are they firm, do they bleed on palpation? Is there pus exuding from any areas? The presence of pus indicates a more serious problem than gingivitis and immediate referral to a dentist must be sought.

Clinical parameter of bleeding on probing is a reliable tool for diagnosing gingival inflammation, whereas the clinical sign of non-bleeding on probing is not a safe criteria for evaluating gingival health.

A dentist will use a "periodontal probe" to measure the sulcular depth. The most common procedure of measuring sulcular depths is to use a periodontal probe, and note the depths on a periodontal chart. This may be used for baseline charting or further investigations of causes of increased depths. A depth of the gingival sulcus more than 2 mm may be indicative of periodontal disease.
There is no role of radiography and culture in the diagnosis and management of gingivitis.
If there is erythematous friable tissue at the gum line, gingivitis is confirmed.
If it is simple gingivitis, it can be controlled by improving oral hygiene.
For complicated gingivitis refer to dentist for further treatment.
Gingivitis secondary to a systemic disorder or other underlying etiology requires treatment of the underlying cause.
Recommend personal plaque control in conjunction with professional removal of plaque, calculus, and other contributing factors. C
Antibiotics are useful in rapidly lowering counts of periodontal pathogens. C
Antibiotic treatment is not recommended for the routine treatment of gingivitis.

However, prophylactic antibiotics reduce the probability of infection by 70% in patients undergoing third molar extractions (for periodontal infection or severe caries), and reduced the risk of dry socket and post-procedure pain in such patients.
Many mouthwashes are available for plaque control. However, these must be used in conjunction with mechanical removal of plaque.
Chlorhexidine gluconate (CHX) is the most effective anti-plaque agent.
Regular use of chewing gums containing CHX may reduce dental plaque formation as well.
Many mouthwashes and toothpastes have other anti-plaque agents including quaternary ammonium compounds, which are also effective.
Studies have shown that open debridement is more effective in the removal of subgingival accretions from root surfaces in areas with pockets of 6 mm or greater.
Surgery is not recommended in people with factors such as poor plaque control, smoking, and uncontrolled diabetes since that may have adverse effects on the outcome of the surgery.
In patients with above risk factors, a 3-month supportive periodontal recall program and nonsurgical management are recommended.
Surgical treatment is not usually indicated in patients with gingivitis unless there are gingival pockets that are interfering with plaque control, function, or esthetics.

Herbal mouthwash containing the pericarp extract of Garcinia mangostana may be used as an adjunct in treating oral malodour. The use of this mouthwash showed a statistically significant reduction in both the plaque index and papillary bleeding index after 2 weeks.
Educate patient regarding the etiology of gingivitis and risk factors for disease progression and give patients oral hygiene instructions.
Replacement of missing restorations or treatment of any immediately needed restorations, removal of over hang fillings, endodontic therapy, and extraction of "hopeless teeth."
Refer patients who continue to show signs of periodontitis, bleeding on probing, purulence, or any signs of disease progression.
Patients should be referred to a primary care dentist for initial evaluation.
Untreated gingivitis will usually progress and eventually lead to tooth loss. Prognosis is good with treatment, though. C
Follow up should be at 3, 4 and 6 months of interval for maintenance. C
Treating peridontal disease is associated with improved glycemic control in diabetics, as evidenced by a 0.29% decrease in A1c for up to 4 months. Evidence for an effect after 4 months is lacking.

The presence of periodontitis is associated with chronic kidney disease (OR = 1.65), and a positive association between periodontal treatment and the estimated GFR has been seen in observational studies.
It is common to observe profound yet asymptomatic untreated dental disease in an older person’s mouth.
The teeth of an older person are typically less sensitive or wholly insensitive to temperature changes and to the sensations that commonly herald dental disease in younger adults.
Older dentate adults should have regular dental follow ups every 6 to 12 months.
By the age of 50 years, more than 90% of Americans with teeth, show 2 mm or more of loss of alveolar height. This is a primary marker of prior periodontal disease activity.
There is an association between Gram-negative pneumonia, Gram-negative periodontal pathogens, salivary hypofunction, and impaired swallowing.
Children should be guided to adapt good dental behavior to prevent decay.
Diet modification should include reduced amounts of non-milk extrinsic sugars. Foods and drinks containing sugar should be avoided before bedtime.
Provision of fluoride, which could be from diet, drug therapy, or toothpaste.
For maximum benefit children should spit not rinse after brushing.
Young children should be supervised when brushing teeth.
